Regarding His saying, may He be exalted, in this verse: ﴿and your spouses﴾, the scholars of tafsir (exegesis) have two opinions. The first is that what is meant by "their spouses" is their peers and their likes in obedience and the fear of Allah, and Ibn Kathir confined himself to this view.

The second is that what is meant by "their spouses" is their wives in the Garden, because this latter view is more expressive of luxury and enjoyment than the first.

For this reason, the Qur'an frequently mentions the honouring of the people of the Garden by being with their wives, rather than the favour bestowed upon them by being with their peers and those like them in obedience.

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, they and their spouses, in shade, reclining on couches.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 55-56]

Many scholars said that what is meant by the "busyness" mentioned in the verse is the deflowering of virgins. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We will marry them to houris with beautiful eyes.﴾ [al-Tur: 20] He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And houris with beautiful eyes, like preserved pearls.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22-23] He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Therein are good and beautiful companions... houris, cloistered in pavilions.﴾ [al-Rahman: 70-72] And He said: ﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, with beautiful eyes.﴾ [al-Saffat: 48] (p-143) And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, of equal age.﴾ [Sad: 52] And other verses besides these.

We have already noted that the singular of "azwaj" (spouses) is "zawj" without a ta' (ـة), and that "zawjah" (wife) with the ta' is a valid usage in the language and not a solecism, contrary to those who claim that "zawjah" is a solecism of the jurists and that it has no basis in the language.

The truth is that it is an Arabic usage, and from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And indeed he who strives to corrupt my wife is like one who goes to a lion's den to take its ..."

And the saying of al-Hamasi:

"My daughters wept out of grief for her, and my wife, while those who were departing toward me then parted."

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said about Safiyyah: "Indeed she is my wife."

As for His saying ﴿delighted﴾ (tuhbarun), the views of the scholars concerning it all go back to one thing, namely that they are honoured with the greatest and most complete kinds of honour.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on Surah 43, verse 71:**

Allah's words: ﴿They will be served with platters of gold﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this. All the verses in which Allah mentions the bounties granted to the people of Paradise, namely vessels of gold and silver, adornment with them, and wearing silk, including *al-sundus* and *al-istabraq*, are of this kind. In Surat al-Nahl, in the discussion of His words ﴿and you extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾ [al-Nahl: 14], this was also covered.

* *

Allah's words: ﴿And therein is whatever the souls desire and that which the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide eternally﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, mentions that everything the souls desire and that the eyes take delight in, that is, that the eyes find pleasure in by seeing its beauty, as He said: ﴿Yellow, its color bright, pleasing to the observers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 69]. He attributed the pleasure to the eye, though in reality it belongs to the owner of the eye, just as lying and sin are attributed to the forelock, which is the front of the hair of the head, in His words: ﴿a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 16], and as humility, labor and toil are attributed to faces in His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, laboring and exhausted﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2–3].

It is known that lying and sin are in reality attributed to the owner of the forelock, just as humility, labor and toil are attributed to the owners of the faces.

What this noble verse indicates, that in Paradise there is everything desired and everything pleasant, has come expounded, with its kinds made clear, in many verses of the Book of Allah. It has also come in summary form, comprehensive of every kind of bounty.

As for the summary of this, it is in His words: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17].

As for the detailed explanation of this, the Qur'an has clarified that among the bounties mentioned in the verse are drinks, foods, spouses, couches and thrones, vessels, kinds of ornaments and garments, servants, and other things. We will mention some verses that indicate each of these.

As for foods, Allah said: ﴿For you therein is abundant fruit, from which you eat﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 73]. He said: ﴿And the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 21]. He said: ﴿And fruit in abundance, neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 32–33]. He said: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in resemblance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. And other verses besides these.

As for drinks, Allah said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor, a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth in abundance﴾ [al-Insan: 5–6]. He said: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is of ginger, a spring therein named Salsabil﴾ [al-Insan: 17–18]. His words: ﴿There will go around them young boys made eternal, with cups and jugs and a cup from a flowing spring, they will not be affected by headache from it nor will they be intoxicated﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17–19]. He said: ﴿There will be circulated among them a cup from a flowing spring, white, delicious to the drinkers, without intoxication in it, nor will they be exhausted by it﴾ [al-Saffat: 45–47]. He said: ﴿In it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey, and for them therein is every kind of fruit﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. He said: ﴿Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you put forward in the past days﴾ [al-Haqqah: 24]. And other verses besides these.

As for garments, vessels and ornaments, we have already discussed them fully in Surat al-Nahl.

As for spouses, we have already mentioned some verses indicating them shortly before, and they are many, such as His words: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. What we have mentioned of this shortly before is sufficient.

As for what they recline upon of couches, thrones and the like, it is in many verses, such as:

• His words: ﴿Reclining upon couches whose linings are of brocade﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

• His words: ﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining upon couches﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56].

• His words: ﴿Upon thrones woven [with gold]﴾, ﴿reclining upon them, facing one another﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15–16].

The thrones *al-mawdunah* (مَوْضُونَة) are those woven with rods of gold.

• His words: ﴿As brothers, on thrones facing one another﴾ [al-Hijr: 47].

• His words: ﴿Therein are raised thrones﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 13].

• His words: ﴿Reclining upon green cushions and beautiful carpets﴾ [al-Rahman: 76].

And other verses besides these.

As for their servants, Allah said concerning this: ﴿There will go around them young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]. He said in Surat al-Insan, describing these youths: ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan: 19]. He mentioned the bounty of the people of Paradise in the most emphatic form in His words: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bounty and a great kingdom﴾ [al-Insan: 20].

The verses indicating the kinds of bounty of Paradise, its beauty and perfection, such as shades, springs, rivers and other things, are very many, and we will suffice with what we have mentioned.

As for His words in this noble verse: ﴿And you therein will abide eternally﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71], we have already presented the clarifying verses, because their eternity mentioned here has absolutely no cessation, such as:

• His words: ﴿A gift not cut off﴾ [Hud: 108], meaning not discontinued,

• His words: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54].

• His words: ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah is enduring﴾ [al-Nahl: 96].

(p-146) We have already discussed this noble verse and similar verses that indicate that deeds are a cause of entering Paradise,

- like His saying: ﴿And it is called out to them, "This is the Paradise you have been made to inherit because of what you used to do."﴾ [al-A'raf: 43].
- And His saying: ﴿That is the Paradise which We give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing.﴾ [Maryam: 63].
- And His saying: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17].

We have also explained the closest ways of reconciling these noble verses and what is similar in meaning with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and grace."

We have mentioned in this regard that the deed which the verses show to be the cause of entering Paradise is the deed that Allah accepts by His mercy and grace, and that the deed which does not admit a person to Paradise is the deed that Allah does not accept.

And Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 27].

The Words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾

The lam in His words "li-yaqḍi" (let... put an end) is the lam of supplication (lam al-du'a').

The apparent meaning is that their intention by this is to ask Malik, the keeper of the Fire, to supplicate Allah on their behalf for death.

The evidence for this is two matters. The first: if they had intended to call upon Allah Himself to cause them to die, they would not have called out, "O Malik," and they would not have addressed Him in their words "your Lord."

The second: Allah explained in Surah "al-Mu'min" that the people of the Fire ask the keepers of the Fire to call upon Allah for them, so that He may lighten the punishment for them. This is in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment."﴾ [Ghafir: 49]. And His words "let your Lord put an end to us" means "let Him cause us to die, so that we may find rest in death from the punishment."

A parallel to this is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So Moses struck him and finished him off﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], meaning he caused him to die.

His words, Exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿He will say, "Indeed, you will remain"﴾ are evidence that they will not be granted death, but will remain in the Fire being punished without end.

The Great Qur'an has indicated that they will not die therein so that they might rest through death, that the Fire will not spare them, that its punishment will not be lightened for them, and that they will not come out of it.

As for their not dying therein, which His words here indicate, "Indeed, you will remain," it is indicated by verses of the Book of Allah,

• such as His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74].

• and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And the most wretched will avoid it, who will burn in the greatest Fire, then he will neither die therein nor live﴾ [al-A'la: 11–13].

• and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And for those who disbelieve is the fire of Hell; it will not be decreed upon them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36], to the end of the verse.

• and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and death will come to him from every place, but he will not be dead﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], to the end of the verse.

As for the Fire not sparing them, Allah explained it by His words: ﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase for them the blaze﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. Whoever claims that the Fire has a final subsiding and an end, is refuted by this noble verse.

As for the punishment not being lightened for them, many verses indicate it, very many,

• such as His words: ﴿And its punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ [Fatir: 36].

• and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So it will not be lightened for them, and they will not be given respite﴾ [al-Nahl: 85].

• and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So We will not increase you except in punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 30].

• and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Zukhruf: 75].

• and His words: ﴿Indeed, its punishment was ever a permanent torment﴾ [al-Furqan: 65].

• and His words: ﴿So it will be an inseparable punishment﴾ [al-Furqan: 77],

according to the more correct view regarding the last two.

As for their not being brought out of it, this has come clarified in verses of the Book of Allah,

• such as His words, Exalted is He, in "al-Baqarah": ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them, and they will not be ones who exit the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167].

• and His words, Exalted is He, in "al-Ma'idah": ﴿They wish to exit the Fire, but they will not be ones who exit it, and for them is a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 37].

• and His words, Exalted is He, in "al-Hajj": ﴿Every time they wish to exit from it, out of distress, they are returned into it﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Hajj: 22].

• and His words, Exalted is He, in "al-Sajdah": ﴿Every time they wish to exit from it, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20].

• and His words, Exalted is He, in "al-Jathiyah": ﴿So today they will not be brought out of it, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 35].

And other verses besides these.

We have clarified this topic thoroughly in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab," in Surah "al-An'am," in the discussion of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He will say, "The Fire is your abode, abiding therein, except what Allah wills"﴾ [al-An'am: 128]. And in Surah "al-Naba'," in the discussion of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Remaining therein for ages﴾ [al-Naba': 23]. We will also clarify it, Allah willing, in this blessed book in the discussion of the verse of "al-Naba'" mentioned, and we will there clarify, Allah willing, the removal of a difficulty which the atheists raise against the verses in which this topic is explained.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah "ash-Shura" in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is hard for the polytheists what you call them to.﴾ [Ash-Shura: 13].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this matter in this noble surah, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded and they will be questioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 9]. We have also given many verses clarifying this in Surah Maryam, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! We shall record what he says﴾ [Maryam: 79], and the verse that follows it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 81 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of "in" (inn, "if") in this verse.

A group of the people of knowledge said: it is conditional (shartiyyah). This was chosen by more than one scholar, and among those who chose it is Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Those who said it is conditional differed concerning the intended meaning of His saying: "then I would be the first of the worshippers."

Some of them said: "then I would be the first of the worshippers" of that child.

Some of them said: "then I would be the first of the worshippers of Allah," on the supposition that He has a son.

Some of them said: "then I would be the first of the worshippers of Allah," firmly believing that it is impossible for Him to have a son.

Another group said: the particle "in" in the verse is negative (nafiyah).

The meaning is: "There was not to Allah a son." On the view that it is negative, then concerning His saying "then I would be the first of the worshippers" there are three aspects:

The first, which is the closest of them, is that the meaning is: "There was not to Allah a son; so I am the first of the worshippers of Allah, who declare Him far above having a son, and above everything that does not befit His perfection and majesty."

The second: that the meaning of His saying "then I would be the first of the worshippers" is: "the first of those who are disdainful (āninīn) and who shun (mustankifīn) that," meaning the false saying fabricated against our Lord, which is the claim that He has a son.

The Arabs say: "ʿabida" (with a kasra on the bā') "yaʿbadu" (with a fatha on it), so he is "ʿabid" (with fatha then kasra), by analogy; and "ʿābid" also by usage, when his disdain, shunning and anger become intense. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Those are my people: if they satirize me, I satirize them; and I disdain (aʿbidu) to satirize Kulayb with Darim."

So His saying "wa-aʿbidu" means "I am disdainful (ānifu) and I shun (astankifu)."

From it also is the saying of another:

"Whenever the one who has affection wills, he cuts off his friend, and he will certainly disdain (yaʿbadu) against him, unjustly."

And in the well-known story of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him: a woman of Juhayna who had married was brought to him; she had given birth after six months. So ʿUthman sent for her to be stoned, believing that she had been pregnant before the contract, since her delivery was before nine months. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said to him: "Indeed Allah says: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], and He says, glorified and exalted: ﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾ [Luqman: 14]. So there remains from the period for weaning only six months."

So ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, did not disdain (ʿabida) to send for her to be returned and not stoned.

The point of the evidence in the story is: "by Allah, ʿUthman did not disdain (ʿabida)," that is, he did not feel aversion or disdain from returning to the truth.

The third aspect: that the meaning of ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is: "the first of those who deny and refuse that Allah has a son — exalted is He above that, to a great degree."

The one who clarifies it (his author), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me regarding the meaning of this noble verse is that it is necessary to resort to the view that "in" is negative, and that the view that it is conditional cannot be sound in meaning according to the linguistic usage of the Arabic language in which the Qur'an was revealed, even though a group of eminent scholars held it.

We chose that "in" is the negative and not the conditional, and we said that resorting to that is necessary in our view, for four matters:

The first: this view proceeds in accordance with Arabic style in a clear manner, without any difficulty. The use of "in kāna" (if it was) in the sense of "mā kāna" (it was not) is frequent in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, as in His saying: ﴿It was not but a single cry﴾ [Ya-Sin: 29], meaning: "it was not but a single cry."

So your saying, for example, the meaning of the noble verse is: "There was not to Allah a son; so I am the first of the worshippers who submit to the Mighty, the Greatest, who is declared far above having a son, or the first of those who are disdainful and shun that our Lord be described with what does not befit His perfection and majesty, such as ascribing a son to Him, or the deniers who deny that our Lord has a son — exalted is He above that to a great degree." There is no difficulty in it, because it proceeds according to the Arabic language in which the Qur'an was revealed, indicating the complete declaration of Allah's transcendence above having a son, with no possibility whatsoever of implying the contrary.

The second matter: the declaration of Allah's transcendence above having a son by expressions that admit no ambiguity is what many verses in the Qur'an have brought, as we have previously explained in surah "al-Kahf" in the discussion of His saying: ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. And in surah "Maryam" in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." You have certainly produced something monstrous﴾ [Maryam: 88–89]. The many verses we mentioned in this indicate that "in" is negative.

So the clear negation that is not disputed shows that what is intended in the place of dispute is clear negation.

The best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an. The expression in the verse, "There was not to the Most Merciful a son" [al-Zukhruf: 81], in the form of clear negation, agrees with His saying in surah "Bani Isra'il": ﴿And say, "Praise is to Allah, who has not taken a son"﴾ [al-Isra': 111],

• and His saying at the beginning of "al-Furqan": ﴿and has not taken a son and has not had a partner in dominion﴾ [al-Furqan: 2],

• and His saying: ﴿Allah has not taken any son﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91],

• and His saying: ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3],

• and His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their falsehood that they say, "Allah has begotten," and indeed they are liars﴾ [al-Saffat: 151–152],

and to other verses besides these.

As for the view that "in" is conditional, and that His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is the answer (jaza') to that condition, there is absolutely no parallel to this in the Book of Allah, and no verse in it indicates this meaning.

The third matter: the view that "in" is conditional cannot yield any meaning in the Arabic language except a forbidden meaning that may not be held under any circumstances, and the Book of Allah, exalted is He, must be declared free from being interpreted according to forbidden meanings that may not be held.

The explanation of this is that on the view that "in" is conditional, and His saying ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ is the answer of the condition, there is no sense in its truth at all except by the validity of the connection between the condition and the answer.

The certain verification without doubt is that the basis of truth and falsehood in the connected conditional proposition (al-shartiyyah al-muttasilah) rests on the validity of the connection between its antecedent, which is the condition, and its consequent, which is the answer. The decisive proof of this is that a connected conditional may be entirely true while both of its parts are false, or one of them is false, if the particle of connection between its two parts is removed. An example of it being false in both parts while true as a whole is His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. This is a proposition entirely true, as you see, yet if the particle of connection between its two parts were removed, each of its two parts would undoubtedly be a false proposition. By the particle of connection we mean the word "law" (if) from the first part and the lam from the second part; if they were removed and deleted, the first part would become: "in them were gods other than Allah," which is a proposition in the extreme of falsehood, and the second part would become: "they were ruined," i.e., the heavens and the earth, which is a proposition in utter falsehood, as you see.

It thus becomes clear that the basis of truth and falsehood in conditionals rests on the validity of the connection between the two parts and the invalidity of it.

If the connection is valid, the proposition is true, even if its parts or one of them are shown to be false when the connection is removed.

If the connection between them is false, the proposition is false, as when you say: "If this were a human, it would be a stone." The falsity of the connection between them and the falsity of the proposition because of it are both evident.

Examples of the truth of a conditional while both its parts are false are very numerous, such as the verse we mentioned, and such as your saying: "If the human were a stone, he would be a body," and "If the horse were a ruby, it would be a stone." All these propositions and the like are true while both their parts are false if the particle of connection is removed.

An example of its truth while one of them is false is your saying: "If Zayd were in the sky, he would not have escaped death." It is a true conditional because the connection between its two parts is valid, although it is false in one of its parts and not the other: non-escape from death is true, and Zayd's being in the sky is false. Thus al-Banani exemplified with this example; but in my view, the conditional he exemplified with is a conjunctive (ittifaqiyyah), not a necessary (luzumiyyah) conditional, and conjunctives have no place in this topic.

The correct example is: "If the human were a stone, he would be a body."

Know that a group claimed that the basis of truth and falsehood in conditionals rests specifically on the consequent, which is the answer, and that the antecedent, which is the condition, is a restriction on that. They claimed that this meaning is what is intended among the people of the Arabic tongue.

The verification is the first view.

No one at all has stated a third view about the basis of truth and falsehood in conditionals.

Having understood this, know that the noble verse, on the view that it is a conditional and answer sentence, cannot have a valid connection between its two parts under any circumstances, on either of the two views with no third, except in a forbidden manner that may not be held under any circumstances.

The explanation of that: on the last view, that the locus of truth and falsehood in conditionals is only the consequent, which is the answer, while the antecedent, which is the condition, is a restriction on that, the meaning of the verse on it is false, indeed it is disbelief, because its meaning would be that his being the first of the worshippers is conditional upon the Most Merciful having a son, exalted is He above that to a great degree.

Because the implication of the condition is that if He had no son, he would not be the first of the worshippers, and the corruption of this meaning is evident, as you see.

As for the first view, which is the sound one, that the basis of truth and falsehood in conditionals rests on the validity of the connection between the two parts of the conditional:

On the view that the noble verse is a condition and answer sentence, there is also no valid connection between its two parts at all, except in a forbidden way that may not be resorted to under any circumstances. This is because the worshipped being having a son, and his or his son's deserving worship, cannot have any connection between them at all except with a meaning that is disbelief in Allah; for the one who deserves worship cannot be conceived in any way to be a son or a father.

(p-153) By this you know that the alleged condition in His saying "If the Most Merciful had a son" is only attached to something impossible, since it is impossible for the Most Merciful to have a son.

It is known that only the impossible is attached to the impossible.

Thus, making the worship of Allah, which is the foundation of the religion, conditional upon His having a son is evidently corrupt, as you see. A conditional is true in such a case only if the conditioning element were impossible. So the claim that "in" in the verse is conditional is like saying: "If there were with Him gods, I would be the first of the worshippers of Him," and this is never true in any way, because one of a plurality of gods cannot be worshipped. So the connection between its two parts, like this proposition, cannot be valid under any circumstances.

This becomes clear to you from the meaning of His saying: ﴿And there was not with Him any god; otherwise each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

For His saying "otherwise" (idhan) means: if there were with Him other gods, each one of them would have taken away what he created and become independent with it, some of them would have overpowered others, no order would have been established for the heavens and the earth, and everything would have been corrupted, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22], and His saying: ﴿Say: If there were with Him gods, as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra': 42], according to the sound view, which is the truth among the two interpretations.

The meaning of their seeking a way to Him, exalted is He, is their seeking a path to contend with Him, as some kings do with one another.

The conclusion: if an impossible thing is made the condition, then the connection between it and the answer cannot be valid, unless the answer is also impossible; for an impossible condition can only produce an impossible answer.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 81 (part 2 of 4):

As for the condition being impossible while the consequent is the foundation of the religion and the pillar of the matter, this cannot be correct in any way.

Whoever holds this view among the scholars and the religious figures is undoubtedly mistaken.

There is no doubt that every conditional statement (shartiyyah) in which the antecedent, which is the condition (shart), is false and its consequent (tali), which is the result (jaza'), is true, when the connection is removed, cannot be used as an example for this verse in any way. What al-Fakhr al-Razi supposed about the validity of using it as an example is undoubtedly a gross error on his part. The clarification of this is that every conditional statement whose condition is false and whose consequent is true, when the connection is removed, must have one of two things as its basis, with no third possibility at all.

In both cases, the truth [of the statement] arises from a specific matter that cannot be found in the noble verse we are discussing. Rather, it contradicts the meaning of the verse.

Inferring the existence of one of two contradictories from the existence of the other is necessarily invalid. By the first of the two mentioned matters we mean that the conditional statement is a coincidental (ittifaqiyyah) conditional and not a necessary (luzumiyyah) conditional at all.

By the second of them we mean that the truth mentioned arises from the particular subject matter (khusus al-madda).

It is known that truth arising from the particular subject matter carries no weight in rational matters, and that it is equivalent to falsehood because it is not consistent: it is true in one matter and false in another.

What is considered is only the necessary, consistent truth that does not vary with the subject matter in any way.

There is no doubt that every proposition whose condition is impossible has a consistently true consequent only if its consequent is also impossible in particular.

If a proposition is found whose condition is false and whose consequent is correct, then this must be, either because it is coincidental, or because of the particular subject matter alone.

An example of this occurring because it is coincidental is your saying: "If Zayd is in the sky, he has not escaped death."

Here the condition, which is his being in the sky, is false, and the consequent, which is his not having escaped death, is true.

This is correct only because this conditional is coincidental.

It is known that a coincidental conditional has no connection at all between its two parts, so the affirmation or negation of one does not entail the affirmation or negation of the other. There is no relation between its two parts in meaning at all; it exists only in wording.

Zayd's being in the sky has no connection at all to his not escaping death, and there is no link between them except in wording. It is like your saying: "If man is rational, then the horse neighs."

We have already explained the difference between the necessary conditional and the coincidental conditional in surah al-Kahf, in discussing His saying: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, then, ever﴾ [al-Kahf: 57]. Refer back to it there.

It is known that no one has said that His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ is a coincidental conditional, and no one has claimed that there is no connection at all between its two parts.

An example of this occurring because of the particular subject matter alone is what al-Fakhr al-Razi gave as an example for this noble verse, without noticing the extreme incompatibility between the noble verse and what he gave as an example for it. When he said: the condition, which is ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, is false, and the consequent, which is ﴿then I am the first of the worshippers﴾, is true,

he illustrated this with his saying: "If man is a stone, then he is a body." He meant that his saying "If man is a stone" is a false condition, just as His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ is. So man's being a stone and the Most Merciful's having a son are both false conditions.

Since the consequent that follows the false condition in his saying "If man is a stone, then he is a body" is true, this shows that the true consequent in His saying ﴿then I am the first of the worshippers﴾ can be placed after the false condition which is ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾.

This is a very gross error and an equating of two utterly contradictory things. The consequent that follows the false condition in his saying "If man is a stone, then he is a body" is true only because of the particular subject matter, not because of any meaning that the connection requires at all.

The clarification of this is that the relation between body and stone, and the relation between man and body, are both general and specific absolute (al-'umum wal-khusus al-mutlaq) in each case.

Body is absolutely more general than stone, and stone is absolutely more specific than body. Likewise, body is more general than man in an absolute sense, and man is more specific than body in an absolute sense. So body is the proximate genus (jins qarib) of stone and a remote genus (jins ba'id) of man. If you wish, you may say it is an intermediate genus (jins mutawassit) for him.

The clarification of this is that you say in the first division: body is either growing (nami), i.e., it grows gradually, or non-growing. Non-growing things, such as stone for example, are of this kind. Then you divide the growing into a second division, saying: the growing is either sensitive (hassas) or non-sensitive. The non-sensitive among them is like plants.

Then you divide the sensitive into a third division, saying: the sensitive is either rational (natiq) or non-rational. The rational among them is man.

It becomes clear that both man and stone fall under the generality of body, and a judgment about the more general concerning the more specific is true in affirmation without dispute or detail.

So your saying "Man is a body" is true in every composition, and it cannot be falsified in any way. This is because of the special association between them: body is the genus of man, and man is an individual of the species of body. Because of this particular association between them, the judgment that man is a body is true in every case, whether the judgment is not contingent on anything, or is contingent on something false or true.

So the inference: this example confirms the truth of the connection between the condition and the consequent in His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first of the worshippers﴾, its falsity being as plain as the sun at the fourth hour of the day.

How extremely strange it is that any intelligent person would say this! For the example given is true only because man falls under the meaning of body.

As for one who has a son, the relation between him and the true God is one of opposition of contradiction (tabayun al-muqabala), because the opposition between the God who is worthy of worship and a father or a son is the opposition between a thing and the equal of its contradictory. For whoever is born, or has a child born to him, cannot possibly be a God worthy of worship in any way.

The clarification of the incompatibility between the two matters is that if you say "Man is a body," you speak the truth, but if you say "The one who has a child is a god," or "The born one is a god," you speak the falsehood which is outright disbelief (al-kufr al-bawah).

Among what clarifies what we have mentioned is the consensus of all the theologians (nuzzar) that if one of the two premises of an argument is false while the conclusion is true, then this occurs only because of the particular subject matter, and that this truth carries no weight. Its judgment is the judgment of falsehood, and only the necessary, consistent truth in all circumstances is considered.

So if you say, for example: "Every man is a stone, and every stone is a body," then the first figure yields the conclusion "Every man is a body," and this conclusion is entirely true, as you see.

Yet the minor premise of the argument, which is your saying "Every man is a stone," is wholly false, as you see.

The conclusion is true only because of the particular subject matter, as we have explained. Otherwise it would be false, since the conclusion is a necessary consequence of the argument, and truth cannot be a necessary consequence of falsehood. If any such thing happens, it is because of the particular subject matter, as we have explained.

By this verification you know that a false condition does not necessarily entail, and that its connection holds consistently only with a false consequent of the same kind.

As for what some scholars suppose, that His saying ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Scripture before you﴾ [Yunus: 94] is like His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first of the worshippers﴾, this is a gross error. The difference between the meanings of the two verses is vast, so the supposition that they are equal in meaning is false.

The clarification of this is that His saying ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, and so on, has an intended meaning that follows Arabic usage, with no ambiguity in it. For we have already explained that the truth of a conditional statement depends on the validity of the connection between its condition and its consequent. It is true even if both its parts are false when the connection is removed, as explained shortly before.

So the connecting of His saying ﴿if you are in doubt﴾ with His saying ﴿ask those who read the Scripture﴾ is a valid connection with no problem in it, because the one who is in doubt about a matter is, as is well known, to ask one who knows about it. So it is a true proposition, even though its condition and its consequent are each false when taken separately. It is like His saying ﴿If there had been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. It is a true conditional because the connection between its two parts is valid, even though both parts are false when the connection is removed.

As for His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first of the worshippers﴾, on the view that "in" (in) is a conditional particle, there can be no valid connection at all between its condition and its consequent, because the connection between a God worthy of worship and being a father or a son is never valid in any way.

For this reason it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask the People of the Book." Thus he negated both parts, even though the connection is valid. Neither he nor anyone else could negate both parts in the other verse, so neither he nor anyone else would say: "He has no son, and I do not worship him."

In any case, the connection between doubt and the doubter's asking one who knows is a valid matter, unlike the connection between worship and the worshipped being a father or a son, which is not valid.

The difference between the two verses is thus clear. The hadith "I do not doubt, nor do I ask the People of the Book" was transmitted by Qatadah ibn Di'amah as a mursal report (one whose chain omits a companion).

Something similar was said by some of the Companions and those after them, and its meaning is undoubtedly correct.

What al-Zamakhshari said in interpreting this noble verse is something every reader finds strange, because of its ugliness and monstrousness. I do not know of any unbeliever, among those whom Allah mentions in His Book, who would dare to say the like of it or anything close to it. And this is in addition to his not understanding what he is saying and the contradiction in his speech.

Here we will mention his ugly words, to draw attention to the enormity of his religious and linguistic error.

He said in the Kashshaf, and its text is: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and that were established and proven by a sound proof that you bring and a clear argument that you put forward, then I am the first [to] magnify that son and to be the first to submit to him and obey him, just as a man magnifies the son of a king out of reverence for his father.

This is a statement given as a supposition and an illustration for a purpose, namely to emphasize the negation of a son and to elaborate on it, so that no doubt is left for the one who speaks it except one that is entirely dissolved, together with a declaration of his own position by affirming pre-eternity (al-qidam) in the chapter on monotheism. He made worship dependent on the existence of a son, which is impossible in itself, so what was made dependent on it is impossible like it. So it is in the form of affirming existence and worship, and in meaning it negates both, in the most forceful and emphatic way.

A parallel to this is that a Qadarite (al-'adli) says to a determinist (al-mujabbir): "If God, may He be exalted, creates unbelief in hearts and punishes for it with an everlasting punishment, then I am the first to say: He is a devil, and not a god."

The meaning of this statement, and what its wording and structure were designed for, is the negation that God, may He be exalted, is the creator of unbelief, and His transcendence and sanctification above that. But this is by way of emphasizing it in the manner we have mentioned, together with indicating the leniency of the doctrine and the misguidance of the one who holds it, the decisive testimony to its impossibility, and the declaration of his own disavowal of it and his utmost aversion and revulsion toward committing it.

Similar to this manner is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah have mercy on him, to al-Hajjaj when he said to him: "By Allah, I will replace you in this world with a blazing fire." He replied: "If I had known that this was up to you, I would not have worshipped any god other than you."

Al-Shinqiti, Adwa' al-Bayan, on surah 43, verse 81 (part 3 of 4):

People have strained themselves to draw out of this noble style, which is full of subtle points and benefits and which by itself establishes tawhid in its most eloquent forms, the meaning: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers" — [i.e.,] the monotheists who worship Allah alone, who deny your saying that the Most Merciful has a son. Thus it is said: ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾ according to your claim, ﴿then I am the first of the worshippers﴾, the monotheists of Allah, who deny your saying that a son is ascribed to Him. End of quotation (ha).

This is the purpose of al-Zamakhshari's words.

In these words of his there is ignorance of Allah and extreme audacity toward Him, as well as confusion and self-contradiction regarding the linguistic meanings — what Allah alone knows.

I do not think this is hidden from any intelligent person who reflects upon it.

We shall explain to you what makes this clear. He first said: ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and he clarified this with a sound proof you would present and a clear argument by which you would offer evidence, ([then I am the first]) to magnify that son and to be the first of you to submit to him and obey him, just as a man magnifies the son of a king out of reverence for his father.

His statement is therefore plainly false to any intelligent person, because on the supposition that a son is correctly attributed to Him, and a sound proof and clear argument stand that He has a son, there is no doubt that this requires that the son does not deserve worship in any way, even if there were in that a magnification of his father; for his father is like him in not deserving worship, and disbelief in the worship of every parent and every begotten one is a condition of the faith of every monotheist. So in what respect would this statement be correct?

As for the Arabic language, it is not correct at all.

I do not think it is correct in any non-Arabic language either; the linking of this condition to this consequent is not valid in any respect.

Thus the meaning of the verse on this reading is not valid in any respect, because what is conditioned upon the impossible must itself be impossible like it.

(p-160) Al-Zamakhshari, in his words, whenever he wished to give an example from outside the verse, was compelled to make the conditional attach only to what is, in his view, impossible.

So his illustration of the verse by the story of Ibn Jubayr with al-Hajjaj is clear evidence of what we have mentioned and of his self-contradiction and confusion.

For he said in it: al-Hajjaj said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "I will surely replace you in this world with a fire that blazes."

Sa'id said to al-Hajjaj: "Had I known that this was in your hands, I would not have worshipped any god other than you."

This shows that he attached the impossible to the impossible. Had he not been contradicting the meaning for which al-Zamakhshari cited it, he would have said: "Had I known that this was in your hands, I would have been the first of those who worship Allah."

So his statement, "Had I known that this was in your hands," has the same sense as ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, and attributing a son or a partner to Him are equal in impossibility and in the claim of deficiency.

If Sa'id had understood the verse in your false manner, he would have said: "Had I known that this was in your hands, I would have been the first of those who worship Allah."

But he did not say this, because it has no sound meaning to which one may turn.

Likewise is al-Zamakhshari's illustration of the noble verse in his ugly, hideous, repugnant words, which every disbeliever would shrink from uttering.

In it he was also compelled to attach only a monstrous impossibility, in his view, to the impossible. For he said therein: "Its parallel is that the Adli says to the Mujbir: If Allah the Exalted is the creator of disbelief in hearts and punishes for it with everlasting torment, then I am the first to say He is a devil and not a god."

Look at the words of this misguided man in his illustration of the meaning of this noble verse by the words of the misguided one whom he calls the Adli: "If Allah is the creator of disbelief in hearts..." and so on.

The creation by Allah of disbelief in hearts and His punishing the disbelievers for their disbelief is, in his view, impossible, just as attributing a son to Allah is impossible. Yet this impossibility, in his false claim, he attached to the most monstrous kind of impossibility (p-161), which is his vile claim that if Allah is the creator of disbelief in hearts and punishes for it, then He is a devil and not a god, glorified is He above what the wrongdoers say, exalted to a great height.

Look, may Allah have mercy on you, at the enormity of this man's ignorance of Allah and the severity of his self-contradiction regarding the Arabic meaning of the verse.

For he made his saying "If Allah is the creator of disbelief and punishes for it" equivalent to ﴿If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, in that the condition in both is impossible; and he made his saying about Allah, that He is a devil and not a god, glorified is He above what the wrongdoers say, exalted to a great height.

Like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the first of the worshippers."

So the necessary consequence of his words would be that he says: "If He were the creator of disbelief, then I am the first of those who worship Him." It is not hidden that the claim against Allah that He is a devil contradicts his saying: "then I am the first of the worshippers."

I have turned away from lengthening the explanation of the falsity of his words, the severity of his misguidance and his self-contradiction, because of their ugliness and the clarity of their falsity. They are ornate phrases and a flood of words with no benefit in them, and they carry within them disbelief, ignorance of the Arabic meaning of the verse, and clear contradiction. How many a speech is filled with ornamented language and yet is barren, with no benefit or substance in it, as it has been said:

"And I, and I, then I, and I..."
"When my sandal strap broke, I made for it a thong, and it kept being used for days."
And he compared water after toil to water...

Know that the discussion of predestination and the creation of the acts of servants: we have already presented sufficient portions of it in this surah, in the commentary on His saying the Exalted: ﴿And they say: If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 20]. And it is not hidden that the Qur'an explicitly states that Allah the Exalted is the Creator of all things, as He said: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 16], and He said: ﴿And He created everything and determined it with precise measure﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]. He said: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah?﴾ [Fatir: 3]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

Thus belief in predestination, its good and its evil, which is one of the creeds of the Muslims, al-Zamakhshari made to imply that Allah has a devil — glory be to Allah, exalted above what al-Zamakhshari says, to a great height.

(p-162) May Allah repay al-Zamakhshari with what he deserves.

The fourth matter: the inductive survey of the Mighty Qur'an shows that when Allah the Exalted wishes to posit the impossible in order to clarify the truth by positing it, He attaches it first to the particle that indicates its non-existence, which is the word (law, "if only"), and He attaches to it nothing but a comparable impossibility:

• As in His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22].
• And His saying the Exalted: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen whom He willed from among what He creates﴾ [az-Zumar: 4].
• And His saying the Exalted: ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence﴾ [al-Anbiya': 17].

As for attaching this to a particle that does not imply its non-existence, such as the word (in, "if") where the consequent is not impossible, this is not customary in the Qur'an.

Among what clarifies the meaning we have mentioned is the exchange reported by a group of exegetes between al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Although its chains are not sound, its linguistic meaning is correct.

It is that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So Allah revealed His saying: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son﴾, to the end of the verse.

Al-Nadr said to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira: "Do you not see that he has confirmed me?"

Al-Walid said: "No, he has not confirmed you; rather he says: 'The Most Merciful had no son, so I am the first of the worshippers,' that is, the monotheists of the people of Makkah who exalt Him above having a son." So the exchange of these two disbelievers, who knew Arabic, agrees with what we have established.

For al-Nadr said that the meaning of the verse, taking (in) as conditional, agrees with what the disbelievers believe about ascribing a son to Allah, and this is a forbidden meaning; and al-Walid said that (in) is negative, and that the meaning of the verse on that reading is opposing the disbelievers and exalting Allah above having a son.

By all that we have mentioned it becomes clear that (in) in the noble verse is negative.

This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Zuhayr ibn Muhammad and others.

* *

(p-163) Caution.

Know that what Ibn Jarir and others besides him said, that the view that (in) is negative necessarily implies the forbidden notion which is not permissible regarding Allah, is mistaken.

They said: for if the meaning is "Allah had no son," it negates a son only in the past; so the disbelievers could say: "Then you have spoken truly; He had no son in the past. But a son came to Him afterward when He intermarried with the jinn, and they bore Him daughters, who are the angels."

This forbidden notion prevents taking it as negation, and there is no doubt of its unsoundness, because the Qur'anic verses abundantly show that this implication has no effect. Had it had an effect, Allah would not praise Himself with praise using the word (kana, "was") which denotes specifically past time, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah was Mighty and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa': 158]. ﴿And Allah was Knowing and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa': 17]. ﴿And Allah was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa': 96]. ﴿And Allah was over all things Competent﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27]. ﴿Indeed Allah was High and Great﴾ [an-Nisa': 34]. And other verses that are hard to enumerate.

For the meaning of all those verses is that He was and has not ceased to be.

Had the disbelievers said what they claimed, namely: "You have spoken truly; he had no son in the past, but one arose for Him," they would have said the same about the verses we mentioned.

As if they said: "He was Knowing and Wise" in the past, but there arose for Him the lack of that. And so in all the verses mentioned and the like.

Moreover, the forbidden notion they alleged did not prevent the absolute negation of past existence in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64].

• And His saying: ﴿And I would not take those who mislead as supporters﴾ [al-Kahf: 51].
• And His saying: ﴿And We were not to destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas: 59].

Verses of this kind are numerous.

Among the clearest of them concerning the point in dispute is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And there was not with Him any god﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

Nor did it prevent the Qur'an from negating a son for Him in past time in His saying: ﴿Allah has not taken any son﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. (p-164) For the disbelievers never said at any time: "You have spoken truly; He did not take one in the past, but taking one arose for Him."

Likewise in His saying: ﴿And He has not taken a son﴾ [al-Isra': 111], and His saying: ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3]; because (lam) transfers the present tense to the meaning of the past.

The disbelievers never said: "You have spoken truly; He did not take a son in the past, but taking one arose for Him," nor did they say: "He did not beget in the past, but He begot recently."

The upshot is that the disbelievers never acknowledged that Allah is exalted above having a son, neither in the past, nor in the present, nor in the future.

It is known that the alleged begetting is a restricted event.

By this you know that what they alleged, that the implication of the forbidden notion arises from (in) being negative in the verse, has no foundation and no reliance. And what they claimed, that it is conditional, has no meaning in the Arabic language except the forbidden meaning which is not permissible regarding Allah in any way.

Know that al-Fakhr al-Razi's statement on this noble verse, which implies the possibility of linking its two parts as a conditional, is undoubtedly erroneous in that respect.

As for his refutation of the one who said that the meaning is: "If the Most Merciful had a son according to your claim, then I am the first of the worshippers of Him and the deniers of you in that," this refutation is sound, and his words on it are very good and precise, and they imply its refutation by themselves, against everything he was establishing regarding the noble verse.

The upshot is that the meaning of (in) in the noble verse being negation is free of any problem, any forbidden notion, or any implication, and the Qur'anic verses bear witness to it, because of the abundance of verses consistent with this meaning in the Qur'an.

Now, as for the claim that the meaning of the verse is conditional (al-shart wal-jaza'), this has no meaning in the language that is free of objection, and the Book of Allah contains no parallel to it. This is because the Arabic speakers agree that the meaning differs between conditional with *in* (إنْ, "if") and conditional with *law* (لَوْ, "had"),

because conditional with *law* indicates the absence of the condition, and the absence of the condition necessarily entails the absence of what is conditioned, unlike *in*.

(p-165) Thus, conditional with *in* indicates doubt about the existence of the condition, without dispute.

Whatever departs from this in the use of *in*, where the existence or the non-existence of the condition is known, is due to other reasons and external evidences, and it is not permissible to interpret it as one of the two meanings mentioned, except by a separate proof, as we have explained elsewhere.

* *

**Note (tanbih)**

Know that what we have mentioned, that *law* requires the non-existence of the condition and *in* requires doubt about it, is not refuted by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [Yunus: 94], as we pointed out shortly before.

This is because the truth is that the address in His saying ﴿if you are in doubt﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is whoever among his community could possibly doubt that.

We have already presented, in the discussion of His saying ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾ [Al-Isra': 22] in Surat Bani Isra'il, the clear evidence of the Qur'an that the address from Allah is directed to him (ﷺ), while what is meant is legislation for his community, and he (ﷺ) himself is by no means meant by that address.

We also mentioned there that among the most explicit Qur'anic verses on this is His saying: ﴿And to parents, good treatment. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, say not to them, "uff"﴾ [Al-Isra': 23]. The truth is that the address is to him (ﷺ), while what is meant is his community, not himself, because he is the one who legislates for them by the command of Allah.

The explanation of this, or its meaning: ﴿whether they reach old age with you﴾, that is, if your parents or one of them reach old age with you, O Prophet of Allah, then do not say to them "uff."

It is known that his father died while he was in the womb, and his mother died while he was a child, so it is not possible that what is meant is: if they or one of them reach old age with you. Indeed, both had died long before that.

By this it is established that what is meant by the address is someone other than him from his community, who can live to see his parents or one of them reach old age with him.

We have already stated that this is a well-known Arabic style, and we cited as evidence the rajaz verses of Sahl ibn Malik al-Fazari, in his saying: (p-166)

*O sister of the best of the desert and the settled, how do you see the young man of Fazara?*
*He has come to love a free, perfumed woman. — I mean you, and listen, O neighbour.*

We have expanded the story there, and we showed that the view of those who say that the address in His saying ﴿whether one or both of them reach old age with you﴾ [Al-Isra': 23] is to everyone among his community whose address is valid, not to him himself, is false, by the evidence of His saying after it in the context of the verses: ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾ [Al-Isra': 39].

The conclusion is that the verse ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [Yunus: 94] does not break the rule we have mentioned, because it is like His saying: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾ [Al-Isra': 22]; ﴿If you were to associate others with Him, your deeds would surely be lost﴾ [Al-Zumar: 65]; ﴿So never be among the doubters﴾ [Yunus: 94]; ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 48]; ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [Al-Insan: 24], and other verses.

It is known that he (ﷺ) never does any of those things at all, but he is commanded and forbidden so that he may legislate for his community through his tongue.

By this you know the consistency of the rule we have mentioned regarding the particles *law* and *in*, and that it is not broken by this verse.

This is what has appeared to us regarding this noble verse, and there is no doubt that there is no objection in it, nor any uncertainty, nor any ambiguity. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, far above what they describe.﴾

We have already mentioned the meaning of the word subhan (Glory/Exaltation, i.e., the declaration of God's transcendence above everything that does not befit His perfection and majesty), what it indicates of God's exemption from all that is unfitting to His perfection and majesty, and the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the word subhan along with some Arabic evidences, at the beginning of surah "Bani Isra'il".

When He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ and so on, He declared His own transcendence completely above what they attribute to Him of ascribing a son to Him, clarifying that the Lord of the heavens and the earth and the Lord of the Throne is worthy of being exempt from having a son, and from everything that does not befit His perfection and majesty.

What this noble verse contains, namely that when He mentioned the disbelievers' description of Him with what does not befit Him, He declared His own transcendence above that, informing His creation in His Book that they should declare Him transcendent above everything that does not befit Him, has a similar meaning stated clearly in many verses:

- Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has not taken any son, and there is no god with Him... Glory be to God above what they describe, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91-92]

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He far above what they say, a great elevation.﴾ [al-Isra: 42-43]

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there were in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than God, they would both have been corrupted. So glory be to God, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]

- And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs.﴾ [al-Nisa: 171]

And other verses besides these.

Allah's saying: ﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and play until they encounter their Day which they are promised.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah "al-Hijr," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them﴾ [al-Hijr: 3].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 84:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾.

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in the beginning of Surat al-An'am, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open﴾ [al-An'am: 3], and so on.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾.

This conjunction together with the indefinite form in this verse leads the ignorant person to imagine a plurality of gods, although the Qur'anic verses explicitly state that He is one, such as His saying: ﴿So know that there is no god except Allah﴾ [Muhammad: 19], and His saying: ﴿And there is no god except one God﴾ [5:73], and so on.

The answer is that the meaning of the verse is that He, may He be exalted, is the one worshipped by the people of the heavens and the earth. So His saying: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven﴾ means: worshipped alone in the heaven, just as He is the one truly worshipped on the earth, glory be to Him and exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾.

We have already explained the clarifying verses in Surah "al-An'am" in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 59].

And in "al-A'raf," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal its time except Him"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and in other places.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 86:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him possess no intercession﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah "al-Baqarah," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], and in other places as well.

(p-168) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And if you were to ask them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah," so how are they deluded?﴾

We have already presented, at length, the verses that clarify this matter in Surah Bani Isra'il (Surah al-Isra'), in the discussion of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 88:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And [the Prophet's] saying, "O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe."﴾

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read this word as (wa-qīlahu), with a fatha on the lam and a damma on the ha'. 'Asim and Hamzah read it as (wa-qīlihi), with a kasra on the lam and the ha'.

Some scholars said: its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that it is a conjunction of location (ʿaṭf maḥall) upon (al-sāʿah, "the Hour"), because the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85] contains a verbal noun (maṣdar) that is attached to its object.

So the word al-sāʿah is in the genitive in form by virtue of the annexation (iḍāfah), and in the accusative in location by virtue of being the object. Whatever is like this, its follower may be in the accusative, taking account of the location, or in the genitive, taking account of the form. As he said in the Khulasah (Ibn Malik's Alfiyyah, the summary of grammar): "The follower of what is genitive is made genitive; and whoever considers the location in agreement, it is good."

And he said, regarding its counterpart in the adjective: "Put in the genitive or make accusative the follower of what was put in the genitive, like 'seeking rank and wealth, whoever rises'."

Some others said: it is conjoined to (sirrahum, "their secret"), [al-Zukhruf: 80].

Accordingly, the meaning is: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80]. ﴿And his saying, "O my Lord..."﴾ and so on.

Some others said: it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq).

That is, he said "qīlahu," and it has the meaning of "qawlihi" (his saying), except that when the qaf was given a kasra, the waw was replaced by a ya' for harmony with the kasra.

They said: a parallel to this construction is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*"The slanderers walk on both its sides, and their saying (qaylahum): 'Indeed you, O son of Abi Sulma, are surely to be killed.'"*

That is, "and they say their saying."

(p-169) Some others said: it is in the accusative, governed by a deleted verb (ya'lamu, "He knows"); because the conjunction we mentioned upon His saying "sirrahum," and the conjunction upon "al-sāʿah," it is said of the latter that it requires separating the conjunct from the conjunct-upon by something that cannot serve as a parenthetical insertion, whereas positing the governing verb when the context indicates it presents no difficulty. As he said in the Khulasah: "The governing word may be deleted if it is known, and its deletion may sometimes be obligatory."

As for the reading with the genitive, it is conjoined upon "al-sāʿah," meaning: "And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and the knowledge of his saying, 'O my Lord.'"

Al-Zamakhshari chose that it is genitive by an oath (al-qasam), and its remoteness is not hidden, as Abu Hayyan pointed out.

The verification is that the pronoun in (qīlihi) refers to the Prophet ﷺ.

The evidence for this is that His saying after it: ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 89] is an address to him ﷺ without dispute. So the claim that the pronoun in (qīlihi) refers to Jesus has no evidence and no basis.

What this noble verse contains of his complaint ﷺ to his Lord about his people's unbelief has come clarified in other places, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Messenger said, "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned"﴾ [al-Furqan: 30]. A similar statement is reported of Musa in His saying, the Exalted, in "al-Dukhan": ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "These are a people who are criminals"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 22]. And of Nuh, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have called my people night and day, but my calling has only increased them in flight"﴾ [Nuh: 5-6], to the end of the verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 43, verse 89:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace," for they are going to know.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this letter as ﴿fasawfa yaʿlamūn﴾ (fa-sawfa yaʿlamūna, with the ya' of the third person, "they will know"). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it as (fasawfa taʿlamūn) with the ta' of address, "you will know."

This noble verse contains three matters. The first: His command to him (ﷺ) to pardon (al-safh, i.e., overlooking) the disbelievers.

The second: that he should say to them, "Peace" (salam).

(p-170) The third: a warning to the disbelievers that they will come to know the reality of the matter and the truth of what the disbeliever is promised of the punishment of the Fire.

These three matters have been clarified in other places, such as His saying, exalted is He, regarding the first: ﴿And indeed, the Hour is coming, so overlook with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and disregard their harm﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48] (as rendered in the source's citation, al-Hajj: 48).

Al-safh (pardon) is turning away from taking someone to account for a sin.

Some of them said: it is more emphatic than 'afw (pardon).

They said: this is because the root of al-safh is derived from ṣafḥat al-ʿunuq (the side of the neck), as though he turns toward the wrongdoer with the side of his neck, turning away from rebuking him and what is beyond that.

As for the second matter: Allah has clarified that this is the manner of His righteous servants.

It is well known that he (ﷺ) is their leader, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us are our deeds and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant"﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. And He said concerning Ibrahim: his father said to him: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46]. He said to him: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [Maryam: 47].

The meaning of salam in the mentioned verses is informing them of the safety of the disbelievers from their harm, and from repaying them with evil; that is, "You are safe from us; we will not revile you, nor treat you with the like of what you do to us."

As for the third matter, which is the warning to the disbelievers that they will come to know the truth, it has been clarified in the verses of the Book of Allah,

• such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a time﴾ [Sad: 88].

• And His saying: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know﴾ [al-An'am: 67].

• And His saying: ﴿No! They will come to know. Then no! They will come to know﴾ [al-Naba': 4-5].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! You will come to know. Then no! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3-4].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire. Then you will surely see it with the certainty of sight﴾ [al-Takathur: 6-7].

And other verses besides these.

(p-171) Many people of knowledge say that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So overlook them﴾ and what is in its meaning, is abrogated (mansukh) by the verses of the sword. Groups of the verifying scholars say that it is not abrogated.

Fighting in the place where fighting is obligatory, and overlooking the ignorant and turning away from them, is a noble attribute and a heavenly courtesy, and there is no contradiction between these. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.
